Continuous IV infusion in heart failure: wedge-pressure effect held to 8 h, gone by 12-24 h (Elkayam 1987, 3113764); 51% of the peak wedge-pressure effect lost at 24 h (Dakak 1990, 2118301); right atrial pressure back to control at 24 h while 40-50% of the wedge, SVR and cardiac-index effect remained (Makhoul 1990, 2112336); plasma NTG constant at 5.5 ng/mL as exercise benefit fell to placebo by 24 h, so pharmacodynamic (Zimrin 1988, 3131041); full effect kept by 12 h on / 12 h off (Packer 1987, 3114637) and tolerance partly reversed 8 h after stopping (Dupuis 1990, 2117845), so it recovers: an attenuation that does not recover would be wrong. notes: No model fitted. At constant plasma alfentanil (bolus 50 mcg/kg, 155 mcg/kg/h) 50% of the analgesic effect was lost in 81 +/- 26 min (tail pressure) and 88 +/- 38 min (hot plate; back near saline by 240 min); motor effect (rotarod) 374 +/- 46 min. Holding analgesia constant, alfentanil use rose 50% in 255 +/- 98 and 203 +/- 116 min (Table 1): the potency loss directly, P = 1.5 at about 4 h. Against Vinik and Kissin 1998 (same lab, analgesia, 129-138 min in volunteers) the implied time exponent is 0.08, not 0.25 (which predicts 331-360 min).

notes: Between-system negative feedback on the effect, not a potency shift: Eout = Ed + E0 - Ef, dEf/dt = kg1 (G1 Eout - Ef); G1 1.16 (SE 0.09), kg1 0.0995 (0.0081) /min; EC50 845 ng/mL, gamma 1.85, ke0 4.0 /min. At steady state the effect is 1/(1+G1) = 46% of naive (the abstract's 'diminished by 46%' reads the other way), reached at rate kg1(1+G1), half-time 3.2 min (the paper's 7.0 min is ln2/kg1). An EEG adaptation an order of magnitude faster than analgesic tolerance in the same species (Kissin 1996); not the endpoint for the opioid panel. Needs a 'feedback' structure the panel does not have.
